context_blurb:
A pebble sinks in a pond, yet a cargo ship of steel stays afloat with a full load. What decides is not size or weight alone but how heavy a thing is for its size, which scientists call density. Comparing densities explains floating ships, rising balloons and lakes that freeze only on top.

Density is how much mass, the amount of matter, is packed into each bit of volume, the space a thing takes up. It belongs to the material, not to the size of the piece. A chip broken off a big quartz crystal has far less mass, but it takes up far less room too, in just the same proportion, so its density is the same, since it is the same quartz.

A thing floats in a fluid, any liquid or gas, when it is less dense than that fluid, and sinks when it is denser. The fluid's upward push on a floating thing is called buoyancy.

Even a metal can be the fluid. Mercury is the only metal that stays liquid at room temperature. An iron bolt floats on mercury because mercury is denser than iron. Size is not the reason: the same bolt sinks at once in water. Gold, denser than mercury, sinks in it.

Steel is nearly eight times as dense as water, so a lump of steel sinks straight down. A ship's steel, though, is spread thin around a huge hollow hull full of air. What counts is the whole ship, steel and air together, and its air-filled hull makes it less dense than water, so it floats. Try it with clay: a ball of clay sinks, but the same clay pressed into a boat shape floats.

The fluid's own density matters too. Salt dissolved in seawater adds mass without adding as much volume, so salt water is denser than fresh water, and a swimmer lying on her back floats higher in the sea than in a freshwater lake. The denser the water, the less of it a floating body must push aside to be held up. In the Dead Sea, about ten times saltier than the ocean, people float with no effort at all.

Water holds one more surprise. For most materials the solid form is denser than the liquid, but ice is less dense than the water it freezes from, because freezing locks its particles into an open pattern that takes up more room. So ice floats as a lid on a lake, slowing the lake's loss of heat to the cold air, and the water below stays liquid for the fish. If ice sank like most solids, each new layer formed at the cold surface would drop and pile up on the bottom, with no lid to hold the warmth in, and a shallow lake could freeze from the bottom up.

Air is a fluid too, so the same rule works in the sky. A helium balloon rises because helium is far less dense than air, only about a seventh as dense. Helium does have weight, yet a balloon of it, rubber and all, still floats up. Not every gas rises: carbon dioxide is denser than air and flows along the ground into low places.
